species: turtle (Chrysemys picta and Pseudemys rubriventris), bull-frog, and grass frog
readout_other: mechanical (kymograph) recording of heart rate, contraction amplitude and tone; graphic recording of skeletal/smooth-muscle twitches; comparison with electrical stimulation.
direction_notes: High-intensity 340 kHz sound waves caused rhythmic contraction of quiescent turtle/frog ventricle and a faster, lower-amplitude auricular rhythm; weak sub-minimal twitching was also produced in nerve-containing skeletal muscle (abolished by curarization) and some contraction in smooth muscle, both much weaker than the cardiac effect.

exposures.label: Turtle and frog heart (auricle and quiescent ventricle) immersed in Ringer's solution

target.label: heart muscle (auricle and ventricle) of turtle and frog

timing.protocol_description: A 2 kilowatt oscillator drove a quartz crystal tuned to 340 kc, transmitting the vibration via oil to a Ringer's-solution bath containing the preparation; a rheostat controlled intensity by varying the crystal voltage, but the paper states that quantitative intensity values cannot be given because they depend on many uncontrollable factors. Exposure was applied and removed by hand while the preparation's response was recorded on a kymograph.

Paper states 'eight hearts in all investigated' for the cardiac experiments but gives no aggregate subject count across the separate nerve/muscle and smooth-muscle experiments (including one curarized frog), so a total is not reported.
Preparations mix excised hearts, excised/immersed nerve-muscle preparations, and one intact curarized frog leg; 'preparation' is used as an approximation.

Paper attributes the (weak) twitching response to the nerve rather than the muscle (curarization abolished it), but the preparation is the sciatic-nerve-innervated gastrocnemius muscle as a whole; also includes turtle neck/leg muscle tested the same way.
